article.title: AWS Continuum Reaches GA With Per-Line, Per-Inference Pricing; Google's CodeMender, Not AWS's Tool, Runs the Behavior-Equivalence Check
article.summary: AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now GA with usage-based pricing; sources show it and Google's CodeMender draw the autonomous-patch trust line differently.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

Amazon Web Services has taken Continuum for code vulnerabilities out of gated preview and into general availability, in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon), according to [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/11/aws-continuum-ga/). The service prices its work by the line of code it watches and by the number of validation steps it runs, and it already offers to open pull requests or upload patch files on a customer's behalf. Google's competing tool, CodeMender, takes a narrower stance on the same question — it still keeps a human reviewer between every generated patch and the codebases it touches. The gap between the two approaches is the clearest evidence yet of where cloud and AI vendors are drawing the line on autonomous code remediation. This analysis keeps what the sources report apart from what follows from comparing them.

## Background

AWS Continuum did not launch as a single product. [InfoQ reported in July 2026](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/07/aws-continuum-code-security/) that it was organized around four agentic capabilities moving at different speeds: penetration testing and code review were "already generally available with established pricing," threat modeling was "in preview," and code vulnerabilities — the capability that builds and ships code patches — was "in gated preview." Chet Kapoor, AWS's VP of search, security, and observability, said at the time that "Continuum is built on lessons learned from running security across AWS and Amazon.com."

AWS's own documentation frames the motivation for the whole Continuum line in terms of an arms race: "Frontier AI models have given attackers new capabilities, such as generating complex exploits from vulnerability disclosures in minutes rather than hours," according to the [AWS Continuum user guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/continuum/latest/userguide/what-is-continuum.html). The same page says Continuum for code vulnerabilities "integrates with GitHub and Amazon S3 for code and context," and that penetration testing and threat modeling are documented separately, under the AWS Security Agent user guide rather than Continuum's own.

## Current Situation

With general availability, Continuum for code vulnerabilities works, per InfoQ's reporting, by building a context graph from a customer's connected code sources, supplemented by what InfoQ calls "an optional collector supplying resource and network context from wherever the code runs." Instead of ranking findings by severity score, InfoQ reports that "Continuum confirms which findings are reachable by running the exploit in an isolated sandbox," producing an attack path and, in the article's words, "a blast radius assessment instead of a risk score alone."

AWS frames the problem this solves as alert fatigue. Christopher Rae, who InfoQ identifies as the AWS executive who "leads AI security go-to-market," said scanners find thousands of findings daily and that "most becomes noise that doesn't matter in your environment," per InfoQ's report.

When Continuum does produce a fix, delivery depends on where the code lives. AWS's documentation on [viewing generated patches](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/continuum/latest/userguide/cv-viewing-patches.html) says that when a customer turns on "Automatically deliver remediation patches" for an environment, "For GitHub, AWS Continuum creates pull requests. For Amazon S3, AWS Continuum uploads patch files under `continuum-patches/` in your bucket." The same page tells customers to "review generated patches to understand the proposed code changes before you apply them," and lets them download a patch file to inspect regardless of whether automatic delivery is on.

AWS's [pricing page for Continuum](https://aws.amazon.com/continuum/pricing/) sets two separate charges for code vulnerabilities. A context fee is billed per million lines of code protected per month, in declining tiers: $200 for the first 10 million lines, $180 for the next 90 million, $160 up to 1 billion, $130 up to 10 billion, and $100 above that. A second, separate inference fee charges $10 per "Continuum inference unit," the page's billing unit for each validation step the service runs. Recalculating from AWS's own tier table, a customer with 100 million lines of code would pay $2,000 for the first 10 million lines plus $16,200 for the next 90 million, for an $18,200 monthly context fee — matching the figure InfoQ arrived at independently. InfoQ's own worked example adds an inference cost for 10,000 vulnerabilities at two inference units each, for $200,000, bringing the same scenario's total to $218,200 a month, or roughly $20 per validated finding. Penetration testing, documented and priced separately, costs $50 per task-hour per AWS's pricing page; InfoQ reports that threat modeling's preview pricing has not yet been published.

## Implications

The sources point to a specific, narrow difference in how AWS and Google have built out their respective automated-patching tools, rather than a difference in ambition. Both companies are trying to solve the same problem — too many vulnerability findings and not enough engineers to triage them — with an agent that reads code, proposes a fix, and tries to prove the fix is real. Where they diverge is in what happens between a generated patch and a merged one.

Google's CodeMender, [according to Google DeepMind's own announcement](https://deepmind.google/discover/blog/introducing-codemender-an-ai-agent-for-code-security/), builds an explicit check for regressions into its pipeline: "an LLM-based critique tool that highlights differences between original and modified code to detect regressions," combined with "differential testing, fuzzing, and SMT solvers for systematic code scrutiny." DeepMind says this is what lets CodeMender claim it has upstreamed "72 security fixes" to open-source projects over six months, on codebases "as large as 4.5 million lines of code," including a fix tied to CVE-2023-4863, a previously exploited libwebp flaw. Even so, DeepMind states plainly that "currently, all CodeMender-generated patches undergo human researcher review before upstream submission" — every patch, without exception, before it reaches a real repository.

AWS Continuum's documented delivery path does not describe an equivalent automated check for whether a generated patch preserves a program's original behavior. Its own instructions ask the customer to review a patch before applying it, but the same documentation describes an opt-in "Automatically deliver remediation patches" setting that opens a GitHub pull request or drops a file into an S3 bucket without that review being a precondition of delivery — review happens, if it happens, inside the customer's own pull-request process rather than inside Continuum itself. InfoQ reports that AWS has said it intends to let Continuum go further, applying certain classes of fix without a human initiating the change once unspecified confidence criteria, such as test coverage and historical success rate, are met; AWS has not published what those criteria are or when that capability might ship.

Neither company's publicly documented position settles which approach is safer at scale — DeepMind's regression-testing claims and AWS's patch-delivery mechanics come from each company's own materials, not from an outside audit of either tool's real-world error rate. What the sources do establish is that the two highest-profile entrants in agentic vulnerability remediation have made different calls on the same design question: whether a human has to look at a generated fix before it can land, or whether that decision is something a customer can delegate to the tool itself.
